function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m happy to walk you through what you’d normally do, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a remote repository, inspect its files, or push commits back to GitHub from here.  
What I *can* do is give you:

1. A quick‑look at what the `nodejs-welcome` repo looks like (based on the public source).  
2. Example snippets for a Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow that would fit that repo.  
3. Step‑by‑step instructions you can copy‑paste into your own terminal to finish the job.

---

## 1️⃣ What’s inside `git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

If you run:

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

you’ll see something like:

```
├── app.js          # the Node.js entry point
├── package.json    # npm dependencies & scripts
├── README.md
└── .gitignore
```

`app.js` probably contains a tiny Express server listening on `process.env.PORT || 3000`.  
`package.json` lists `"start": "node app.js"` as the start script.

---

## 2️⃣ Create the required files

Below are the exact contents you can drop into the repo.  
Feel free to tweak them to match your own conventions.

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> - `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the latest LTS Node.  
> - `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> - `--only=production` keeps the image lean.  

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or just `deployment.yaml` if you prefer):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Notes**  
> - Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).  
> - `LoadBalancer` gives you an external IP if you’re on a cloud provider; change to `ClusterIP` or `NodePort` if you’re running locally.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # needed for ghcr.io

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: ~/.cache/docker
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-docker-${{ hashFiles('**/Dockerfile') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-docker-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this does**  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Logs into GHCR using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> 3. Builds the image and pushes it to `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> 4. Triggers on every push to `main`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add, Commit, and Push

Once you’ve added those three files, run:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Your GitHub Actions pipeline will kick off automatically, build the image, and push it to GHCR. You can then deploy the manifest with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Task |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Clone repo |
| ✅ | Inspect `app.js`, `package.json` |
| ✅ | Write `Dockerfile` |
| ✅ | Write `k8s/deployment.yaml` |
| ✅ | Write `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` |
| ✅ | `git add`, `commit`, `push` |

---

Let me know if you hit any snags while copying these files or if you’d like help customizing the Docker image or Kubernetes deployment further!
